title: Domain Name System Structure and Delegation
summary: Provides information on how names in the Domain Name System are structured, especially the top-level domains, and on how administration of domains is delegated. It is informational and does not define a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1591 describes the structure of DNS top-level domains and who administers them. It sets out principles for choosing domain managers, who are responsible for serving the domain's community.

questions: how is the dns name space structured
what are the rules for delegating a domain
what is a designated manager in dns
subtitle: How DNS names are organized and how responsibility for domains is delegated.

tldr.problem: The growing DNS name space required rules for the top-level domains and for assigning responsibility to domain managers.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes generic and country-code top-level domains and gives six principles for appointing and transferring designated managers.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, not a standard. It describes managers as trustees serving the community and applies the principles to subdomain delegations.

today: RFC 1591 is an Informational memo published in March 1994, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its descriptions record the domain policy and registry structure stated in the memo.

sections.title: DNS Administration
sections.content:
The memo describes IANA as the overall authority for IP addresses, domain names, and other Internet parameters. Day-to-day assignment of addresses, autonomous system numbers, and most top- and second-level domain names is handled by the Internet Registry and regional registries.

In the memo's description, the central Internet Registry is INTERNIC.NET. It names RIPE NCC as the regional registry for Europe and APNIC for Asia-Pacific, while the InterNIC administers North America and regions not yet delegated.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA coordinates the overall name system, while registries handle much of its daily administration. The memo also describes regional registries and the responsibilities assigned to them at that time.

sections.title: Top-Level Domains
sections.content:
The DNS root is unnamed. The memo lists seven generic top-level domains: EDU, COM, NET, ORG, GOV, MIL, and INT. It also describes two-letter country-code domains based on ISO 3166. The memo says it is extremely unlikely that other top-level domains will be created.

Five generic domains are described as international: COM, EDU, NET, ORG, and INT. GOV and MIL are limited to the United States. Country-code domains may use different structures and may delegate parts of their name trees to other managers.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS names begin below an unnamed root with a top-level domain, such as a generic label or a country code. Each top-level domain can organize and delegate names in its own way.

sections.title: Choosing a Designated Manager
sections.content:
Each domain needs a designated manager with administrative and technical contacts. For a country-code top-level domain, at least the administrative contact must live in the country. The manager is a trustee serving the community, not an owner of the domain.

The manager must apply fair rules without favoring related customers or requiring a particular product. Significantly interested parties should agree on the manager; if they cannot, the memo describes review by the Internet DNS Names Review Board. A manager must operate the DNS competently, including primary and secondary name servers. A transfer requires agreement from both the old and new organizations.
sections.plainLanguage: A designated manager is responsible for operating a domain on behalf of its community. The memo requires fair treatment, competent operation, and agreement when responsibility is transferred.

sections.title: Names, Trademarks, and Country Codes
sections.content:
The memo says that a domain registration does not grant trademark status. If registrants dispute a name, the registration authority's role is limited to providing each party with the other's contact information; the requestor must ensure the name does not violate another party's trademark.

IANA does not decide which places count as countries. The memo uses the ISO 3166 list because ISO has a procedure for determining which entities are included.
sections.plainLanguage: Registering a domain name does not give it trademark status. The memo also says IANA relies on ISO's country list rather than deciding what is a country.

sections.title: Status and Security
sections.content: RFC 1591 says it provides information for the Internet community and does not specify an Internet standard. Its security section says that security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo describes domain administration rather than setting a technical standard. It does not discuss security issues.
